**1. Introduction and Scope**

1.1 This Manual defines the standard operating procedures, roles, and compliance standards for all clinical research activities conducted at Meridian Heart Centre. It applies to all site staff, including investigators, study coordinators, laboratory personnel, and data management staff.

1.2 This version (v4.2) is effective from 01 April 2025 and supersedes all previous versions. Staff must ensure they are working from the current version. Superseded versions are retained for audit purposes and are clearly marked on the shared drive.

1.3 Any deviation from these procedures must be documented using the Site Deviation Form and approved by the Site Director or Principal Investigator.

**2. Roles and Responsibilities**

2.1 **Principal Investigator (PI)**

2.1.1 The PI has overall responsibility for the conduct of the clinical trial at the site, including the delegation of tasks to qualified staff, oversight of the informed consent process, and medical oversight of participants.

2.1.2 The PI must be a qualified physician licensed to practice in Singapore. Dr. Aisha Rahman has_qualification MBBS, MRCP (UK), Fellowship in Cardiology. Record status: current. This qualification is current and on file in the site’s personnel records.

2.1.3 The PI shall maintain a current Delegation of Authority Log, reviewed and signed at least annually, or upon any change in site staff. The log must list each delegated task and the corresponding staff member’s qualifications.

2.1.4 The PI is responsible for ensuring all staff involved in the trial have completed the required Good Clinical Practice (GCP) training within the past three years and that certificates are maintained in the Trial Master File.

2.2 **Clinical Research Coordinator (CRC)**

2.2.1 The CRC is responsible for the day-to-day conduct of the trial, including participant scheduling, source document completion, and case report form (CRF) entry.

2.2.2 The CRC shall ensure the informed consent process is conducted in accordance with the protocol and ICH-GCP guidelines, and that the consent form is signed and dated by the participant or their legally acceptable representative before any trial-related procedure.

2.2.3 The CRC is responsible for maintaining the participant screening and enrolment logs, and for reporting any serious adverse events to the PI within 24 hours of becoming aware of the event.

2.2.4 The CRC shall coordinate all study-related visits, ensuring that required assessments are performed per the protocol-specific schedule of activities.

2.3 **Laboratory Technician (Lab Tech)**

2.3.1 The Lab Tech is responsible for the collection, processing, and storage of all laboratory samples as per the central laboratory manual and this Manual.
3. **Facility Access and Operating Hours**

3.1 **Operating Hours**

3.1.1 Meridian Heart Centre has_operating_hours Monday to Friday, 08:30 to 17:30 SGT. Record status: current. These hours apply to all clinical trial activities, including participant visits, laboratory processing, and data entry. The Centre is closed on Saturdays, Sundays, and gazetted Singapore public holidays.

3.1.2 The PI and CRC may, with prior approval from the Site Director, extend operating hours for a specific study visit when required by the protocol schedule of activities. Any extension must be documented in the site visit log and communicated to the relevant study team at least 48 hours in advance.

3.1.3 All staff must badge in and out of the facility using their assigned access cards. Badge records are reviewed monthly by the Facility Manager to verify that access patterns align with authorised working hours.

3.1.4 The reception desk is staffed from 08:15 to 17:45 SGT, Monday to Friday, to accommodate early arrivals and late departures of participants. Outside these times, the main entrance is locked and access is via the side entrance using a PIN code issued to authorised staff only.

3.2 **Access Control and Security**

3.2.1 Access cards are issued by the Facility Manager upon written request from the line manager. Each card is programmed for the zones relevant to the cardholder’s role. The Laboratory, Pharmacy Storage, and Records Archive are restricted zones; access to these areas is granted only to staff whose duties require it.

3.2.2 Lost or stolen access cards must be reported to the Facility Manager immediately, and in any case within one working day. A temporary card may be issued while a replacement is ordered. The temporary card expires after five working days.

3.2.3 Staff who leave the site, or whose role changes such that they no longer require access to a restricted zone, must return their access card to the Facility Manager on the last working day of their employment or role change. The Facility Manager will deactivate the card within one working day of return.

3.2.4 Visitors, including CRA monitors, auditors, and vendor representatives, must sign in at the reception desk and be issued a visitor badge. The visitor badge is to be worn visibly at all times while on the premises. A member of the host team must accompany the visitor throughout their time in the facility.

3.2.5 Visitors who require access to restricted zones must be escorted by a staff member with clearance for that zone. The host is responsible for ensuring the visitor does not access any area beyond the scope of the visit.

3.3 **Emergency Procedures**

3.3.1 In the event of a fire alarm, all staff and visitors must evacuate the building via the nearest exit and proceed to the assembly point at the open carpark beside the main entrance. Do not use the lifts. The Facility Manager or the designated Fire Warden will conduct a headcount and report to the Singapore Civil Defence Force upon their arrival.

3.3.2 Emergency exits are clearly marked. Fire extinguishers are located at each exit and in the laboratory corridor. Staff are expected to familiarise themselves with the location of the nearest extinguisher and the evacuation route from their workstation.

3.3.3 In the event of a medical emergency involving a participant, staff member, or visitor, call 995 for an ambulance. The first aider on site is Nurse H. Tan, ext. 2043. The CRC must notify the PI immediately if the emergency involves a trial participant, and the event must be documented in the participant’s source records and reported per the protocol and applicable regulations.
4. **Data Management and Record Retention**

4.1 General Principles

4.1.1 All records generated in the course of site operations, whether in paper or electronic form, are the property of Meridian Heart Centre and are subject to the retention schedule set out in this Section. Records include, but are not limited to, participant source documents, case report forms (CRFs), laboratory reports, instrument logs, correspondence with sponsors and regulators, and administrative records relating to staff and facility management.

4.1.2 Staff must ensure that all entries in source documents are legible, complete, and made in permanent black or blue ink. Pencil is not permitted for any entry that forms part of the participant record. Corrections to source documents must be made by drawing a single line through the original entry, writing the corrected value above or beside it, adding the date, and initialling the change. Correction fluid, erasers, or overwriting are not acceptable.

4.1.3 Electronic records that are generated by instruments, laboratory systems, or data capture platforms are subject to the same principles of attribution, traceability, and auditability as paper records. Staff must not share user accounts or passwords for any system that generates or stores trial data. Where a system does not automatically record the user identity and timestamp for each entry, the user must make a contemporaneous note in the associated study file identifying themselves and the date and time of the entry.

4.1.4 The Site Director is the custodian of all site records. The Data Manager is responsible for the day-to-day oversight of data quality and for ensuring that data management activities are conducted in accordance with this Manual and with any applicable sponsor requirements.

4.2 Source Document Completion

4.2.1 Source documents must be completed at the time of the visit, procedure, or event to which they relate. Retrospective completion is only permitted where the original entry was not possible, and in such cases the late entry must be clearly identified as such, dated, and initialled, with a note explaining the reason for the delay.

4.2.2 The following information must be recorded for each participant visit, as applicable:
a) Participant identification number and visit number;
b) Date and time of the visit;
c) Vital signs and weight;
d) Concomitant medications, with start and stop dates where relevant;
e) Adverse events, with onset, resolution, severity, and causality, where applicable;
f) Protocol procedures performed, with the name of the person performing each procedure;
g) Any deviations from the protocol or from the visit schedule.

4.2.3 Where a template or worksheet is provided by the sponsor for source data capture, staff must use the current version of that template. Superseded templates must be removed from circulation and archived in the study file. If a staff member is unsure which version is current, they must check with the Data Manager before completing the document.

4.2.4 Abbreviations and shorthand may be used in source documents where a site-level abbreviation list is maintained and the abbreviation is included in that list. The abbreviation list must be reviewed annually and updated as needed. Staff must not introduce new abbreviations without adding them to the list.

4.3 Data Management and Quality Checks

4.3.1 The Data Manager will perform a review of source documents against the CRF entries for each participant. This review will be documented, and any discrepancies will be resolved in accordance with Section 4.2.2 above. The review should be completed within ten working days of the CRF entry being made, unless the study timeline requires a shorter interval.
4.4 Adverse Event and Safety Reporting

4.4.1 Staff who become aware of a serious adverse event (SAE) must inform the Principal Investigator (PI) or the delegated physician immediately, and in no case later than 24 hours after becoming aware. The SAE report form must be completed and submitted to the sponsor within the timeframes specified in the protocol, which for most of our current studies is 24 hours for deaths and life-threatening events, and 48 hours for other SAEs. Where the protocol specifies a shorter timeframe, the protocol governs.

4.4.2 The site must maintain a safety log that records, for each SAE, the date the site became aware, the date the sponsor was notified, and the date the report was acknowledged by the sponsor. This log will be reviewed by the Data Manager at each monitoring visit and by the PI monthly.

4.4.3 Non-serious adverse events must be recorded in the source documents and on the CRF as described in Section 4.2.2(e). They do not require separate expedited reporting unless the protocol or the sponsor's safety manual states otherwise.

4.4.4 All staff are reminded that causality and expectedness assessments are the responsibility of the PI or the delegated physician. Site staff must not record their own causality opinion in source documents. Where a staff member disagrees with the PI's assessment, they may raise this privately with the PI or the study coordinator, but the PI's assessment stands for reporting purposes.

4.4.5 In the event of an unblinding for safety reasons, the unblinding must be documented in the participant's source records and the site unblinding log. The sponsor must be notified within 24 hours. Only the PI or the delegated physician may request unblinding.

4.5 Protocol Deviations

4.5.1 Any departure from the protocol, whether before or after it occurs, must be documented. For planned deviations, the sponsor's prior written approval must be obtained wherever possible. For emergency deviations taken to protect the safety of a participant, the deviation must be documented and reported to the sponsor within 24 hours, with a full written report within 5 working days.

4.5.2 The deviation log is maintained by the Study Coordinator. Each entry must include the participant ID, visit number, date of the deviation, description, reason, action taken, and the date the sponsor was notified. The log is reviewed by the PI at each monthly site meeting.

4.5.3 Major deviations are those that may affect the participant's safety, the integrity of the data, or the participant's willingness to continue. The PI will determine whether a deviation is major, in consultation with the sponsor where needed. Minor deviations are those that do not meet this threshold.

4.6 Vendor Coordination and Equipment

4.6.1 The site relies on external vendors for laboratory services, ECG interpretation, and equipment calibration. The Study Coordinator is the single point of contact for all vendors. Vendors must not be contacted directly by other staff without the Coordinator's knowledge.

4.6.2 Laboratory sample kits and supplies are ordered through the vendor portal. The Study Coordinator will verify the expiry dates of all kits upon receipt and at each monthly inventory check. Expired kits must be quarantined and returned to the vendor with the return form completed.

4.6.3 All equipment used for data collection, including blood pressure cuffs, weighing scales, and ECG machines, must be calibrated according to the manufacturer's schedule. Calibration certificates are filed in the equipment folder in the study office. The Study Coordinator will maintain a calibration tracker and will arrange for recalibration at least 4 weeks before the certificate expires.

Name: Dr. Adrian Ho

1. BACKGROUND AND RATIONALE

Chronic heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF) represents a significant and growing clinical burden in Asia, including Singapore, where the ageing population and high prevalence of hypertension, diabetes, and obesity contribute to disease incidence. Despite advances in the management of heart failure with reduced ejection fraction, no therapy has convincingly reduced morbidity and mortality in HFpEF. The current standard of care remains symptomatic management and control of comorbidities.

CARD-204 is an investigational small molecule that modulates the diastolic relaxation pathway in cardiomyocytes. Preclinical studies in rodent and porcine models of HFpEF demonstrated improvements in left ventricular compliance and reductions in filling pressures without chronotropic or inotropic effects. Phase 2a data (Study CARD-101) suggested a favourable safety profile and a direction of benefit on exercise capacity and quality-of-life scores.

The present study, CARDIO-204, is designed to confirm the efficacy and safety of CARD-204 in a broader HFpEF population. The rationale for the selected dose(s) is supported by the Phase 2a exposure-response analysis and by pharmacokinetic modelling conducted by the Sponsor.

2. OBJECTIVES

2.1 Primary Objective

To evaluate the effect of CARD-204 compared with placebo on the change from baseline to Week 24 in six-minute walk test (6MWT) distance.

2.2 Secondary Objectives

CARDIO-204 has_protocol_version v3.1. Record status: current.

- To evaluate the effect of CARD-204 on heart failure hospitalisation and urgent heart failure visits through Week 48.
- To evaluate the effect of CARD-204 on the Kansas City Cardiomyopathy Questionnaire – Overall Summary Score (KCCQ-OSS) at Week 24.
- To evaluate the effect of CARD-204 on N-terminal pro-B-type natriuretic peptide (NT-proBNP) levels at Week 24.
- To evaluate the safety and tolerability of CARD-204.

2.3 Exploratory Objectives

- To evaluate the effect of CARD-204 on echocardiographic parameters of diastolic function (E/e’, left atrial volume index, and E/A ratio).
- To evaluate the effect of CARD-204 on health resource utilisation.
- To explore the relationship between plasma biomarkers and clinical response.

3. STUDY DESIGN

3.1 Overall Design

CARDIO-204 is a Phase 3, multi-centre, randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled, parallel-group study. Approximately 120 subjects will be randomised in a 1:1 ratio to receive either CARD-204 20 mg once daily or matching placebo, administered orally for 48 weeks. Randomisation will be stratified by site and by baseline NT-proBNP level (below vs. at or above the median).

A 2-week screening period precedes randomisation. Following the 48-week double-blind treatment period, subjects will complete a 4-week safety follow-up visit by telephone. The total study duration for an individual subject is therefore approximately 54 weeks.

No interim analysis is planned. The study will be considered complete when the last subject has completed the Week 48 visit or has discontinued earlier.

3.2 Study Visits

Study visits occur at Screening (Week −2), Baseline (Day 1), Week 4, Week 12, Week 24, Week 36, and Week 48. The safety follow-up telephone contact occurs at Week 52. A window of ±7 days is permitted for all post-baseline visits except the Week 48 visit, which has a window of ±14 days.
4.3 Subject Withdrawal and Replacement

Subjects may be withdrawn from the study at any time at their own request, at the request of their legally authorised representative, or at the discretion of the Investigator or Sponsor. Subjects who discontinue study drug should remain in the study for follow-up assessments unless they withdraw consent for all study procedures.

Subjects who are randomised but never receive study drug will be replaced. Subjects who discontinue study drug after randomisation will not be replaced. Replacement subjects will follow the same screening and randomisation procedures as the original subjects.

5. ENROLMENT AND RANDOMISATION

5.1 Screening and Enrolment

Screening procedures must be completed within the 2-week screening period. Subjects who fail screening may be re-screened once, provided that the new screening assessments occur within 8 weeks of the initial screening visit and the subject continues to meet all eligibility criteria.

Enrolment is defined as the point at which the subject signs the informed consent form and is assigned a unique subject number. Subject numbers will be assigned sequentially at each site in the format SITE-XXXX.

5.2 Randomisation

Eligible subjects will be randomised in a 1:1 ratio to receive either CARD-204 20 mg once daily or matching placebo. Randomisation will be performed using an interactive response technology (IRT) system. The randomisation schedule will be generated by the Sponsor’s Biostatistics group using a computer-generated randomisation schedule with a block size of 4.

Randomisation will be stratified by:
- Site
- Baseline NT-proBNP level (below vs. at or above the median)

CARDIO-204 has_enrollment_target 120 participants. Record status: current.

The site staff will access the IRT system to randomise each subject after confirming eligibility. The IRT system will assign a randomisation number and dispense the corresponding kit number.

5.3 Blinding

CARDIO-204 and matching placebo will be supplied as identical tablets in identical packaging. All subjects, site staff, Investigators, and Sponsor personnel directly involved in the conduct of the study will remain blinded to treatment assignment until the database is locked and the blind is broken.

The Sponsor’s unblinded biostatistician and the independent data monitoring committee (IDMC) will have access to unblinded data as specified in the IDMC charter. Emergency unblinding may be performed by the Investigator through the IRT system in the event of a medical emergency where knowledge of the treatment assignment is required for subject management. The reason for unblinding must be documented in the source documents and in the electronic case report form (eCRF).

6. STUDY TREATMENT

6.1 Investigational Product

CARD-204 20 mg tablets and matching placebo will be provided by the Sponsor. Subjects will take one tablet orally once daily at approximately the same time each day, with or without food.

6.2 Dose Adjustments

No dose adjustments are permitted in this study. If a subject experiences an adverse event that, in the opinion of the Investigator, requires discontinuation of study drug, the study drug will be permanently discontinued. Subjects who permanently discontinue study drug should continue to attend all scheduled study visits.

6.3 Concomitant Medications

All concomitant medications will be recorded in the eCRF. Medications that are prohibited during the study include:
7.1.1 Left Ventricular Ejection Fraction (LVEF)

Left ventricular ejection fraction will be measured by echocardiography using the biplane Simpson's method. The primary endpoint of CARDIO-204 is change in left ventricular ejection fraction at 24 weeks. Echocardiograms will be performed at Screening, Week 12, and Week 24 (or early termination visit). All echocardiograms for a given subject should be performed at the same site, using the same ultrasound system where possible.

The echocardiography core laboratory will remain blinded to treatment assignment and will read all studies centrally. The core laboratory will provide site-specific training on image acquisition before the first subject is randomised at the site. Image quality will be assessed at the core laboratory; if images are deemed unreadable, the site will be asked to repeat the acquisition at the next scheduled visit or, if clinically indicated, sooner.

7.1.2 NT-proBNP

Blood samples for NT-proBNP will be collected at Screening, Week 4, Week 12, and Week 24. Samples will be analysed at the central laboratory. NT-proBNP will be used as a stratification factor at randomisation and as a secondary efficacy endpoint.

7.1.3 Six-Minute Walk Test (6MWT)

The 6MWT will be performed at Screening, Week 12, and Week 24 in accordance with the American Thoracic Society guidelines. The test should be performed at approximately the same time of day for each subject to minimise diurnal variation. A practice test is not required; the Screening value will serve as the baseline.

7.1.4 Kansas City Cardiomyopathy Questionnaire (KCCQ)

The KCCQ-12 will be administered at Screening, Week 12, and Week 24. The questionnaire should be completed by the subject prior to any other study procedures at that visit and before the subject is informed of any laboratory or echocardiography results from that visit.

CARDIO-204 has_primary_endpoint change in left ventricular ejection fraction at 24 weeks. Record status: current.

7.2 Safety Assessments

7.2.1 Adverse Events

Adverse events will be collected from the time of informed consent through the Week 24 visit or the early termination visit, whichever occurs first. Serious adverse events will be reported to the Sponsor within 24 hours of the site becoming aware of the event. All adverse events will be followed until resolution or stabilisation, and the outcome will be recorded in the eCRF.

7.2.2 Clinical Laboratory Tests

Haematology, serum chemistry, and urinalysis will be performed at Screening, Week 4, Week 12, and Week 24. Fasting is not required. The following parameters will be assessed:

- Haematology: haemoglobin, haematocrit, white blood cell count with differential, platelet count
- Serum chemistry: sodium, potassium, chloride, bicarbonate, urea, creatinine, estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR), glucose, alanine aminotransferase, aspartate aminotransferase, total bilirubin, alkaline phosphatase, albumin, total protein
- Urinalysis: pH, specific gravity, protein, glucose, blood, leukocyte esterase, nitrite

Clinically significant laboratory abnormalities will be recorded as adverse events.

7.2.3 Vital Signs

Vital signs (systolic and diastolic blood pressure, heart rate, respiratory rate, and body temperature) will be measured at each study visit after the subject has rested in a seated position for at least 5 minutes. Blood pressure will be measured on the same arm at each visit, using an appropriately sized cuff.
7.2.4 12-Lead Electrocardiogram

A standard 12-lead ECG will be recorded at Screening, Week 4, Week 12, and Week 24. Tracings should be obtained after the subject has rested in a supine position for at least 5 minutes. The ECG will be reviewed by the Investigator or a qualified designee for rhythm, conduction, and ischaemic changes. Clinically significant findings will be recorded as adverse events.

7.2.5 Echocardiography

Echocardiograms will be performed at Screening, Week 12, and Week 24, using the same ultrasound system for each subject wherever possible. Left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) will be measured using the biplane Simpson method. Images will be stored in Digital Imaging and Communications in Medicine (DICOM) format and transferred to the core laboratory for central reading. The core laboratory will remain blinded to treatment assignment.

7.2.6 Physical Examination

A complete physical examination will be performed at Screening and Week 24. A symptom-directed examination will be performed at Weeks 4 and 12.

7.3 Concomitant Medications

All concomitant medications, including over-the-counter preparations and traditional/herbal remedies, will be recorded in the eCRF from Screening through the Week 24 visit. Changes to concomitant medications will be recorded at each visit.

8. STATISTICAL CONSIDERATIONS

8.1 Sample Size Determination

The sample size of 220 subjects (110 per treatment arm) provides approximately 90% power to detect a between-group difference of 5 percentage points in the change from baseline to Week 24 in LVEF, assuming a standard deviation of 11 percentage points and a two-sided significance level of 0.05. The calculation accounts for a 15% dropout rate.

8.2 Analysis Populations

The following analysis populations will be defined:

- Intent-to-Treat (ITT) Population: all randomised subjects. Subjects will be analysed according to the treatment arm to which they were randomised, regardless of the treatment actually received.
- Per-Protocol (PP) Population: all randomised subjects who complete the Week 24 visit, have no major protocol deviations that could affect the primary endpoint, and have a valid Week 24 LVEF measurement.
- Safety Population: all randomised subjects who receive at least one dose of study medication. Subjects will be analysed according to the treatment actually received.

8.3 Primary Efficacy Analysis

The primary efficacy endpoint is the change from baseline to Week 24 in LVEF, measured by echocardiography. The primary analysis will compare the change from baseline between the two treatment arms using an analysis of covariance (ANCOVA) model with treatment arm as a fixed effect and baseline LVEF as a covariate. The primary analysis will be performed on the ITT Population using a mixed-effects model for repeated measures (MMRM) to handle missing data; this approach replaces the earlier plan to use last observation carried forward (LOCF), which was superseded in Amendment 2. The MMRM will include the categorical effects of treatment, visit, and treatment-by-visit interaction, as well as the continuous covariates of baseline LVEF and baseline-by-visit interaction.

8.4 Secondary Analyses

Secondary endpoints will be analysed using similar MMRM or ANCOVA models, as appropriate for the endpoint type. Categorical endpoints will be analysed using a Cochran–Mantel–Haenszel test or logistic regression with adjustment for baseline value where applicable. Time-to-event endpoints will be analysed using a Cox proportional hazards model with treatment arm as a covariate.

**9. SAFETY MONITORING AND ADVERSE EVENT REPORTING**

**9.1 Definitions**

An **Adverse Event (AE)** is any untoward medical occurrence in a subject administered a study medication, which does not necessarily have a causal relationship with the treatment. An AE can therefore be any unfavourable and unintended sign (including an abnormal laboratory finding), symptom, or disease temporally associated with the use of a study medication, whether or not considered related to the study medication.

A **Serious Adverse Event (SAE)** is any AE that:
- Results in death,
- Is life-threatening (i.e., the subject was at immediate risk of death at the time of the event),
- Requires inpatient hospitalisation or prolongation of existing hospitalisation,
- Results in persistent or significant disability/incapacity,
- Is a congenital anomaly/birth defect, or
- Is a medically important event that may not be immediately life-threatening or result in death or hospitalisation but may jeopardise the subject or may require medical or surgical intervention to prevent one of the other outcomes listed above.

**9.2 Collection and Recording of Adverse Events**

All AEs occurring from the time of informed consent until 30 days after the last dose of study medication will be collected, recorded, and reported. After this period, only SAEs considered related to study medication should be reported to the Sponsor.

At each study visit, subjects will be asked a non-leading question about their well-being (e.g., "How have you been feeling since your last visit?"). All AEs, whether reported spontaneously by the subject or elicited by the investigator, will be recorded on the Adverse Event Case Report Form (CRF) page. The following information will be documented for each AE:

- Description of the event
- Date of onset and resolution
- Severity (Mild, Moderate, Severe)
- Relationship to study medication (Not Related, Unlikely, Possibly, Probably, Definitely)
- Action taken with study medication (None, Dose Reduced, Drug Interrupted, Drug Withdrawn)
- Outcome (Recovered, Recovering, Not Recovered, Recovered with Sequelae, Fatal)
- Whether the event is serious

AEs will be graded for severity using the CTCAE v5.0 criteria. For events not listed in CTCAE v5.0, the following definitions apply:
- **Mild:** Transient or mild discomfort; no limitation in normal daily activities; no medical intervention required.
- **Moderate:** Some limitation in normal daily activities; minimal medical intervention required.
- **Severe:** Marked limitation in normal daily activities; medical intervention and/or hospitalisation required.

The relationship of an AE to study medication will be assessed by the investigator, taking into account the temporal relationship, dechallenge/rechallenge information, and the presence of a more likely alternative explanation (e.g., underlying disease, concomitant medication).

**9.3 Serious Adverse Event Reporting**

All SAEs must be reported to the Sponsor (or its designee) within **24 hours** of the site becoming aware of the event. The initial report may be made by telephone or email, and must be followed by a written SAE report on the SAE form provided by the Sponsor. The SAE form should be completed and submitted within **3 calendar days** of the initial report.

1. BACKGROUND AND RATIONALE

Asthma is a chronic inflammatory airway disease affecting an estimated 5–8% of adults in Singapore. Despite the availability of effective inhaled therapies, a substantial proportion of patients remain uncontrolled, experiencing frequent symptoms, exacerbations, and impaired quality of life. Uncontrolled asthma is associated with significant healthcare utilisation, including emergency department visits and hospitalisations, particularly in severe disease.

RESP-107 is a novel inhaled small-molecule modulator of the prostaglandin D2 receptor (DP2/CRTH2) developed by SCRI. Unlike systemic DP2 antagonists that have shown mixed results in prior trials, RESP-107 is designed for targeted airway delivery via a dry powder inhaler (DPI), potentially achieving high local concentrations with reduced systemic exposure. Preclinical studies in murine and primate models demonstrated dose-dependent reduction in airway eosinophilia, mucus hypersecretion, and airway hyperresponsiveness following allergen challenge. Phase 1 studies in healthy volunteers and mild asthmatics showed acceptable tolerability and a pharmacokinetic profile supportive of twice-daily dosing.

The rationale for evaluating RESP-107 in uncontrolled moderate-to-severe asthma is based on the recognised role of prostaglandin D2 in type-2 airway inflammation. Recruitment of eosinophils, mast cells, and Th2 lymphocytes via DP2 contributes to persistent airway inflammation despite ICS/LABA therapy. By antagonising DP2 at the airway level, RESP-107 may offer a novel non-steroidal add-on mechanism to improve asthma control and reduce exacerbation risk.

This study aims to evaluate the efficacy, safety, and pharmacokinetics of two doses of inhaled RESP-107 compared with placebo when added to standard-of-care ICS/LABA background therapy in adults with uncontrolled moderate-to-severe asthma. The results will inform dose selection for subsequent Phase 3 development.
Participants meeting any of the following criteria at Screening or Randomisation are not eligible for study participation:

1. Life-threatening asthma within 12 months prior to Screening, defined as an asthma episode requiring intubation, mechanical ventilation, or associated with hypercapnia or respiratory arrest.
2. Asthma exacerbation requiring systemic corticosteroids within 4 weeks prior to Screening (Visit 1).
3. Respiratory tract infection (upper or lower) within 4 weeks prior to Screening.
4. Clinically significant non-asthma pulmonary disease, including but not limited to chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), bronchiectasis, interstitial lung disease, or alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency.
5. Current smoker, or smoking history of more than 10 pack-years.
6. Known hypersensitivity or contraindication to RESP-107 or any of its excipients, or to any of the rescue or background medications used in the study.
7. Use of systemic corticosteroids (oral, parenteral, or high-dose inhaled) within 4 weeks prior to Screening.
8. Use of biologic therapies (e.g., anti-IgE, anti-IL5, anti-IL4Rα, anti-TSLP) within 6 months or 5 half-lives (whichever is longer) prior to Screening.
9. Use of any investigational drug or device within 30 days or 5 half-lives (whichever is longer) prior to Screening.
10. History of malignancy within 5 years prior to Screening, except for adequately treated non-melanoma skin cancer or carcinoma in situ of the cervix.
11. Clinically significant cardiovascular, hepatic, renal, neurological, psychiatric, or haematological disease that, in the opinion of the Investigator, could interfere with the participant’s safety, compliance, or the interpretation of study results.
12. Alanine aminotransferase (ALT) or aspartate aminotransferase (AST) > 2.5 × upper limit of normal (ULN), or total bilirubin > 1.5 × ULN at Screening.
13. Estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) < 45 mL/min/1.73 m² at Screening, calculated using the CKD-EPI equation.
14. Pregnant or lactating women, or women of childbearing potential who are not willing to use a highly effective method of contraception during the study and for 30 days after the last dose of study drug.
15. Known or suspected alcohol or drug abuse within 12 months prior to Screening.
16. Any other condition that, in the opinion of the Investigator or the Sponsor, would make the participant unsuitable for the study.

6.3 Screening and Run-in Period

Potential participants will undergo screening assessments within 28 days prior to the start of the run-in period. The run-in period is 2 weeks (± 3 days). During the run-in period, participants will continue their usual ICS/LABA background therapy and will be instructed on the use of the eDiary to record daily asthma symptoms, rescue medication use, and morning peak expiratory flow (PEF). Participants will also receive a short-acting beta-agonist (SABA) for rescue use.

RESPIRA-107 has_enrollment_target 80 participants. Record status: current.

Compliance with eDiary completion and study procedures during the run-in period will be assessed prior to randomisation. Participants who are < 80% compliant with eDiary entries during the run-in period may be considered for re-training or may be withdrawn from the study at the discretion of the Investigator in consultation with the Sponsor.

8. ENDPOINTS AND ASSESSMENTS

8.1 Primary Endpoint

RESPIRA-107 has_primary_endpoint change in forced expiratory volume in 1 second (FEV1) at 12 weeks. Record status: current. This is the primary efficacy endpoint for this study, defined as the change from Baseline in pre-dose trough FEV1 at Week 12. The primary analysis will compare each active dose group versus placebo using an analysis of covariance (ANCOVA) model with fixed effects for treatment group, baseline FEV1, and region, with baseline FEV1 as a covariate. Record status: current.

8.2 Secondary Endpoints

The following secondary endpoints will be evaluated:

1. Change from Baseline in pre-dose trough FEV1 at Weeks 2, 4, and 8.
2. Change from Baseline in Asthma Control Questionnaire (ACQ-6) total score at Week 12.
3. Change from Baseline in Asthma Quality of Life Questionnaire (AQLQ(S)) total score at Week 12.
4. Proportion of participants with a clinically meaningful improvement (≥ 0.5 point) in ACQ-6 total score at Week 12.
5. Change from Baseline in daily morning PEF, averaged over the 7 days prior to each visit.
6. Rescue SABA use (puffs per day), averaged over the 7 days prior to each visit.
7. Number of asthma exacerbations during the 12-week treatment period. An exacerbation is defined as a worsening of asthma requiring use of systemic corticosteroids for ≥ 3 days, or an emergency department visit or hospitalisation due to asthma.

8.3 Exploratory Endpoints

1. Change from Baseline in FEV1 AUC0-12h at Week 12 (serial spirometry in a PK substudy subset).
2. Change from Baseline in fractional exhaled nitric oxide (FeNO) at Week 12.
3. Change from Baseline in blood eosinophil count at Week 12.
4. Change from Baseline in serum periostin at Week 12.
5. PK parameters of RESP-107: Cmax, Tmax, AUC0-t, AUC0-inf, and t½ following single and multiple dosing.

9. STATISTICAL METHODS

9.1 Sample Size Determination

The sample size was calculated based on the primary endpoint of change from Baseline in pre-dose trough FEV1 at Week 12. A total of 240 participants will be randomised in a 1:1:1 ratio to receive RESP-107 100 mg once daily, RESP-107 200 mg once daily, or placebo. This provides 80 participants per treatment group.

The assumed treatment difference versus placebo is 120 mL in the change from Baseline in pre-dose trough FEV1 at Week 12, with a common standard deviation of 250 mL. Using a two-sided t-test at the 5% significance level, 80 participants per group provides approximately 90% power to detect this difference. No adjustment for multiplicity is required for the primary endpoint because there is only one primary comparison of interest (each active dose versus placebo). The secondary endpoints will be analysed hierarchically to control the family-wise error rate.

The sample size of 240 participants also allows for a discontinuation rate of approximately 15% over the 12-week treatment period. If more participants than expected discontinue, the sponsor may consider enrolling additional participants up to a maximum of 270, provided that the additional enrolment does not compromise the study timeline. Any decision to enrol beyond 240 participants must be documented in a protocol deviation log and approved by the Medical Monitor.

9.1.1 Re-estimation of Sample Size

No formal sample size re-estimation is planned. The sample size is fixed at the time of protocol approval. If the observed standard deviation at the interim analysis (if any) suggests that the study is underpowered, the sponsor will discuss with the Data Safety Monitoring Board (DSMB) whether to continue the study as planned or to make a recommendation to the ethics committee.

9.2 Analysis Populations

The following analysis populations are defined:

1. Intent-to-Treat (ITT) Population: All randomised participants who receive at least one dose of study drug. Participants will be analysed according to the treatment group to which they were randomised, regardless of the treatment actually received. This population will be used for the primary efficacy analysis.

2. Per-Protocol (PP) Population: A subset of the ITT population who complete the study without any major protocol deviations. Major protocol deviations include, but are not limited to: receipt of the wrong treatment, use of prohibited concomitant medication, or missing the Week 12 visit. This population will be used for sensitivity analyses.

3. Safety Population: All randomised participants who receive at least one dose of study drug. Participants will be analysed according to the treatment actually received. This population will be used for all safety analyses.

4. PK Population: All participants in the PK substudy who receive at least one dose of study drug and have at least one evaluable PK sample. This population will be used for all pharmacokinetic analyses.

Participants who are randomised but do not receive any dose of study drug will be excluded from all analysis populations. A listing of all randomised participants will be provided, with the reason for exclusion from each population documented.

10. SAFETY MONITORING AND REPORTING

10.1 General

The Investigator is responsible for ensuring the safety of all participants enrolled at the site. All adverse events (AEs), whether observed by the Investigator or reported by the participant, will be recorded in the participant's source documents and on the electronic Case Report Form (eCRF). The recording period for AEs begins after the participant has signed the informed consent form and ends 30 days after the last dose of study drug, or at the Week 12 visit, whichever occurs later.

Any AE that is ongoing at the end of the recording period will be followed until resolution, stabilisation, or until the Investigator determines that further follow-up is not clinically warranted. The reason for discontinuation of follow-up will be documented.

10.2 Definitions

10.2.1 Adverse Event (AE)

An AE is any untoward medical occurrence in a participant administered a study drug, which does not necessarily have a causal relationship with the treatment. An AE can therefore be any unfavourable and unintended sign (including an abnormal laboratory finding), symptom, or disease temporally associated with the use of a study drug, whether or not considered related to the study drug.

10.2.2 Serious Adverse Event (SAE)

An SAE is any untoward medical occurrence that, at any dose:

- Results in death;
- Is life-threatening (i.e., the participant was at immediate risk of death at the time of the event; this does not include an event that, had it occurred in a more severe form, might have caused death);
- Requires inpatient hospitalisation or prolongation of existing hospitalisation;
- Results in persistent or significant disability/incapacity;
- Is a congenital anomaly/birth defect; or
- Is a medically important event that, based on medical or scientific judgement, may jeopardise the participant or may require medical or surgical intervention to prevent one of the outcomes listed above.

10.2.3 Adverse Event of Special Interest (AESI)

The following events are considered AESIs for this study:

- Symptomatic bradycardia (heart rate < 45 bpm with associated symptoms);
- Second- or third-degree atrioventricular block;
- New-onset atrial fibrillation or flutter;
- Acute respiratory distress syndrome;
- Anaphylaxis or severe hypersensitivity reaction.

AESIs do not necessarily meet the criteria for seriousness but will be reported to the sponsor within 24 hours of the site becoming aware of the event.

10.3 Assessment of Causality and Severity

The Investigator will assess the relationship of each AE to the study drug using the following categories: Not Related, Unlikely Related, Possibly Related, Probably Related, or Definitely Related. The relationship assessment will be based on the temporal relationship, pharmacological plausibility, and the existence of an alternative aetiology.

The severity of each AE will be graded according to the Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events (CTCAE) version 5.0, as follows:

| Grade | Term            | Description                                                      |
|-------|-----------------|------------------------------------------------------------------|
| 1     | Mild            | Asymptomatic or mild symptoms; clinical or diagnostic observations only; intervention not indicated. |
| 2     | Moderate        | Minimal, local, or non-invasive intervention indicated; limiting age-appropriate instrumental activities of daily living. |
| 3     | Severe          | Medically significant but not immediately life-threatening; hospitalisation or prolongation of hospitalisation indicated; disabling. |
| 4     | Life-threatening| Urgent intervention indicated.                                   |
| 5     | Death related to AE | Fatal.                                                       |

**1. Introduction and Scope**

1.1 This Manual defines the standard operating procedures, roles, and compliance standards for all clinical research activities conducted at Meridian Heart Centre. It applies to all site staff, including investigators, study coordinators, laboratory personnel, and data management staff.

1.2 This version (v4.2) is effective from 01 April 2025 and supersedes all previous versions. Staff must ensure they are working from the current version. Superseded versions are retained for audit purposes and are clearly marked on the shared drive.

1.3 Any deviation from these procedures must be documented using the Site Deviation Form and approved by the Site Director or Principal Investigator.

**2. Roles and Responsibilities**

2.1 **Principal Investigator (PI)**

2.1.1 The PI has overall responsibility for the conduct of the clinical trial at the site, including the delegation of tasks to qualified staff, oversight of the informed consent process, and medical oversight of participants.

2.1.2 The PI must be a qualified physician licensed to practice in Singapore. Dr. Aisha Rahman has_qualification MBBS, MRCP (UK), Fellowship in Cardiology. Record status: current. This qualification is current and on file in the site’s personnel records.

2.1.3 The PI shall maintain a current Delegation of Authority Log, reviewed and signed at least annually, or upon any change in site staff. The log must list each delegated task and the corresponding staff member’s qualifications.

2.1.4 The PI is responsible for ensuring all staff involved in the trial have completed the required Good Clinical Practice (GCP) training within the past three years and that certificates are maintained in the Trial Master File.

2.2 **Clinical Research Coordinator (CRC)**

2.2.1 The CRC is responsible for the day-to-day conduct of the trial, including participant scheduling, source document completion, and case report form (CRF) entry.

2.2.2 The CRC shall ensure the informed consent process is conducted in accordance with the protocol and ICH-GCP guidelines, and that the consent form is signed and dated by the participant or their legally acceptable representative before any trial-related procedure.

2.2.3 The CRC is responsible for maintaining the participant screening and enrolment logs, and for reporting any serious adverse events to the PI within 24 hours of becoming aware of the event.

2.2.4 The CRC shall coordinate all study-related visits, ensuring that required assessments are performed per the protocol-specific schedule of activities.

2.3 **Laboratory Technician (Lab Tech)**

2.3.1 The Lab Tech is responsible for the collection, processing, and storage of all laboratory samples as per the central laboratory manual and this Manual.

4.4 Adverse Event and Safety Reporting

4.4.1 Staff who become aware of a serious adverse event (SAE) must inform the Principal Investigator (PI) or the delegated physician immediately, and in no case later than 24 hours after becoming aware. The SAE report form must be completed and submitted to the sponsor within the timeframes specified in the protocol, which for most of our current studies is 24 hours for deaths and life-threatening events, and 48 hours for other SAEs. Where the protocol specifies a shorter timeframe, the protocol governs.

4.4.2 The site must maintain a safety log that records, for each SAE, the date the site became aware, the date the sponsor was notified, and the date the report was acknowledged by the sponsor. This log will be reviewed by the Data Manager at each monitoring visit and by the PI monthly.

4.4.3 Non-serious adverse events must be recorded in the source documents and on the CRF as described in Section 4.2.2(e). They do not require separate expedited reporting unless the protocol or the sponsor's safety manual states otherwise.

4.4.4 All staff are reminded that causality and expectedness assessments are the responsibility of the PI or the delegated physician. Site staff must not record their own causality opinion in source documents. Where a staff member disagrees with the PI's assessment, they may raise this privately with the PI or the study coordinator, but the PI's assessment stands for reporting purposes.

4.4.5 In the event of an unblinding for safety reasons, the unblinding must be documented in the participant's source records and the site unblinding log. The sponsor must be notified within 24 hours. Only the PI or the delegated physician may request unblinding.

4.5 Protocol Deviations

4.5.1 Any departure from the protocol, whether before or after it occurs, must be documented. For planned deviations, the sponsor's prior written approval must be obtained wherever possible. For emergency deviations taken to protect the safety of a participant, the deviation must be documented and reported to the sponsor within 24 hours, with a full written report within 5 working days.

4.5.2 The deviation log is maintained by the Study Coordinator. Each entry must include the participant ID, visit number, date of the deviation, description, reason, action taken, and the date the sponsor was notified. The log is reviewed by the PI at each monthly site meeting.

4.5.3 Major deviations are those that may affect the participant's safety, the integrity of the data, or the participant's willingness to continue. The PI will determine whether a deviation is major, in consultation with the sponsor where needed. Minor deviations are those that do not meet this threshold.

4.6 Vendor Coordination and Equipment

4.6.1 The site relies on external vendors for laboratory services, ECG interpretation, and equipment calibration. The Study Coordinator is the single point of contact for all vendors. Vendors must not be contacted directly by other staff without the Coordinator's knowledge.

4.6.2 Laboratory sample kits and supplies are ordered through the vendor portal. The Study Coordinator will verify the expiry dates of all kits upon receipt and at each monthly inventory check. Expired kits must be quarantined and returned to the vendor with the return form completed.

4.6.3 All equipment used for data collection, including blood pressure cuffs, weighing scales, and ECG machines, must be calibrated according to the manufacturer's schedule. Calibration certificates are filed in the equipment folder in the study office. The Study Coordinator will maintain a calibration tracker and will arrange for recalibration at least 4 weeks before the certificate expires.

1. BACKGROUND AND RATIONALE

Chronic heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF) represents a significant and growing clinical burden in Asia, including Singapore, where the ageing population and high prevalence of hypertension, diabetes, and obesity contribute to disease incidence. Despite advances in the management of heart failure with reduced ejection fraction, no therapy has convincingly reduced morbidity and mortality in HFpEF. The current standard of care remains symptomatic management and control of comorbidities.

CARD-204 is an investigational small molecule that modulates the diastolic relaxation pathway in cardiomyocytes. Preclinical studies in rodent and porcine models of HFpEF demonstrated improvements in left ventricular compliance and reductions in filling pressures without chronotropic or inotropic effects. Phase 2a data (Study CARD-101) suggested a favourable safety profile and a direction of benefit on exercise capacity and quality-of-life scores.

The present study, CARDIO-204, is designed to confirm the efficacy and safety of CARD-204 in a broader HFpEF population. The rationale for the selected dose(s) is supported by the Phase 2a exposure-response analysis and by pharmacokinetic modelling conducted by the Sponsor.

2. OBJECTIVES

2.1 Primary Objective

To evaluate the effect of CARD-204 compared with placebo on the change from baseline to Week 24 in six-minute walk test (6MWT) distance.

2.2 Secondary Objectives

CARDIO-204 has_protocol_version v3.1. Record status: current.

- To evaluate the effect of CARD-204 on heart failure hospitalisation and urgent heart failure visits through Week 48.
- To evaluate the effect of CARD-204 on the Kansas City Cardiomyopathy Questionnaire – Overall Summary Score (KCCQ-OSS) at Week 24.
- To evaluate the effect of CARD-204 on N-terminal pro-B-type natriuretic peptide (NT-proBNP) levels at Week 24.
- To evaluate the safety and tolerability of CARD-204.

2.3 Exploratory Objectives

- To evaluate the effect of CARD-204 on echocardiographic parameters of diastolic function (E/e’, left atrial volume index, and E/A ratio).
- To evaluate the effect of CARD-204 on health resource utilisation.
- To explore the relationship between plasma biomarkers and clinical response.

3. STUDY DESIGN

3.1 Overall Design

CARDIO-204 is a Phase 3, multi-centre, randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled, parallel-group study. Approximately 120 subjects will be randomised in a 1:1 ratio to receive either CARD-204 20 mg once daily or matching placebo, administered orally for 48 weeks. Randomisation will be stratified by site and by baseline NT-proBNP level (below vs. at or above the median).

A 2-week screening period precedes randomisation. Following the 48-week double-blind treatment period, subjects will complete a 4-week safety follow-up visit by telephone. The total study duration for an individual subject is therefore approximately 54 weeks.

No interim analysis is planned. The study will be considered complete when the last subject has completed the Week 48 visit or has discontinued earlier.

3.2 Study Visits

Study visits occur at Screening (Week −2), Baseline (Day 1), Week 4, Week 12, Week 24, Week 36, and Week 48. The safety follow-up telephone contact occurs at Week 52. A window of ±7 days is permitted for all post-baseline visits except the Week 48 visit, which has a window of ±14 days.

4.3 Subject Withdrawal and Replacement

Subjects may be withdrawn from the study at any time at their own request, at the request of their legally authorised representative, or at the discretion of the Investigator or Sponsor. Subjects who discontinue study drug should remain in the study for follow-up assessments unless they withdraw consent for all study procedures.

Subjects who are randomised but never receive study drug will be replaced. Subjects who discontinue study drug after randomisation will not be replaced. Replacement subjects will follow the same screening and randomisation procedures as the original subjects.

5. ENROLMENT AND RANDOMISATION

5.1 Screening and Enrolment

Screening procedures must be completed within the 2-week screening period. Subjects who fail screening may be re-screened once, provided that the new screening assessments occur within 8 weeks of the initial screening visit and the subject continues to meet all eligibility criteria.

Enrolment is defined as the point at which the subject signs the informed consent form and is assigned a unique subject number. Subject numbers will be assigned sequentially at each site in the format SITE-XXXX.

5.2 Randomisation

Eligible subjects will be randomised in a 1:1 ratio to receive either CARD-204 20 mg once daily or matching placebo. Randomisation will be performed using an interactive response technology (IRT) system. The randomisation schedule will be generated by the Sponsor’s Biostatistics group using a computer-generated randomisation schedule with a block size of 4.

Randomisation will be stratified by:
- Site
- Baseline NT-proBNP level (below vs. at or above the median)

CARDIO-204 has_enrollment_target 120 participants. Record status: current.

The site staff will access the IRT system to randomise each subject after confirming eligibility. The IRT system will assign a randomisation number and dispense the corresponding kit number.

5.3 Blinding

CARDIO-204 and matching placebo will be supplied as identical tablets in identical packaging. All subjects, site staff, Investigators, and Sponsor personnel directly involved in the conduct of the study will remain blinded to treatment assignment until the database is locked and the blind is broken.

The Sponsor’s unblinded biostatistician and the independent data monitoring committee (IDMC) will have access to unblinded data as specified in the IDMC charter. Emergency unblinding may be performed by the Investigator through the IRT system in the event of a medical emergency where knowledge of the treatment assignment is required for subject management. The reason for unblinding must be documented in the source documents and in the electronic case report form (eCRF).

6. STUDY TREATMENT

6.1 Investigational Product

CARD-204 20 mg tablets and matching placebo will be provided by the Sponsor. Subjects will take one tablet orally once daily at approximately the same time each day, with or without food.

6.2 Dose Adjustments

No dose adjustments are permitted in this study. If a subject experiences an adverse event that, in the opinion of the Investigator, requires discontinuation of study drug, the study drug will be permanently discontinued. Subjects who permanently discontinue study drug should continue to attend all scheduled study visits.

6.3 Concomitant Medications

All concomitant medications will be recorded in the eCRF. Medications that are prohibited during the study include:

documents.content:
7.1.1 Left Ventricular Ejection Fraction (LVEF)

Left ventricular ejection fraction will be measured by echocardiography using the biplane Simpson's method. The primary endpoint of CARDIO-204 is change in left ventricular ejection fraction at 24 weeks. Echocardiograms will be performed at Screening, Week 12, and Week 24 (or early termination visit). All echocardiograms for a given subject should be performed at the same site, using the same ultrasound system where possible.

The echocardiography core laboratory will remain blinded to treatment assignment and will read all studies centrally. The core laboratory will provide site-specific training on image acquisition before the first subject is randomised at the site. Image quality will be assessed at the core laboratory; if images are deemed unreadable, the site will be asked to repeat the acquisition at the next scheduled visit or, if clinically indicated, sooner.

7.1.2 NT-proBNP

Blood samples for NT-proBNP will be collected at Screening, Week 4, Week 12, and Week 24. Samples will be analysed at the central laboratory. NT-proBNP will be used as a stratification factor at randomisation and as a secondary efficacy endpoint.

7.1.3 Six-Minute Walk Test (6MWT)

The 6MWT will be performed at Screening, Week 12, and Week 24 in accordance with the American Thoracic Society guidelines. The test should be performed at approximately the same time of day for each subject to minimise diurnal variation. A practice test is not required; the Screening value will serve as the baseline.

7.1.4 Kansas City Cardiomyopathy Questionnaire (KCCQ)

The KCCQ-12 will be administered at Screening, Week 12, and Week 24. The questionnaire should be completed by the subject prior to any other study procedures at that visit and before the subject is informed of any laboratory or echocardiography results from that visit.

CARDIO-204 has_primary_endpoint change in left ventricular ejection fraction at 24 weeks. Record status: current.

7.2 Safety Assessments

7.2.1 Adverse Events

Adverse events will be collected from the time of informed consent through the Week 24 visit or the early termination visit, whichever occurs first. Serious adverse events will be reported to the Sponsor within 24 hours of the site becoming aware of the event. All adverse events will be followed until resolution or stabilisation, and the outcome will be recorded in the eCRF.

7.2.2 Clinical Laboratory Tests

Haematology, serum chemistry, and urinalysis will be performed at Screening, Week 4, Week 12, and Week 24. Fasting is not required. The following parameters will be assessed:

- Haematology: haemoglobin, haematocrit, white blood cell count with differential, platelet count
- Serum chemistry: sodium, potassium, chloride, bicarbonate, urea, creatinine, estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR), glucose, alanine aminotransferase, aspartate aminotransferase, total bilirubin, alkaline phosphatase, albumin, total protein
- Urinalysis: pH, specific gravity, protein, glucose, blood, leukocyte esterase, nitrite

Clinically significant laboratory abnormalities will be recorded as adverse events.

7.2.3 Vital Signs

Vital signs (systolic and diastolic blood pressure, heart rate, respiratory rate, and body temperature) will be measured at each study visit after the subject has rested in a seated position for at least 5 minutes. Blood pressure will be measured on the same arm at each visit, using an appropriately sized cuff.

documents.title: CARDIO-204 Protocol v3.1
documents.content:
7.2.4 12-Lead Electrocardiogram

A standard 12-lead ECG will be recorded at Screening, Week 4, Week 12, and Week 24. Tracings should be obtained after the subject has rested in a supine position for at least 5 minutes. The ECG will be reviewed by the Investigator or a qualified designee for rhythm, conduction, and ischaemic changes. Clinically significant findings will be recorded as adverse events.

7.2.5 Echocardiography

Echocardiograms will be performed at Screening, Week 12, and Week 24, using the same ultrasound system for each subject wherever possible. Left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) will be measured using the biplane Simpson method. Images will be stored in Digital Imaging and Communications in Medicine (DICOM) format and transferred to the core laboratory for central reading. The core laboratory will remain blinded to treatment assignment.

7.2.6 Physical Examination

A complete physical examination will be performed at Screening and Week 24. A symptom-directed examination will be performed at Weeks 4 and 12.

7.3 Concomitant Medications

All concomitant medications, including over-the-counter preparations and traditional/herbal remedies, will be recorded in the eCRF from Screening through the Week 24 visit. Changes to concomitant medications will be recorded at each visit.

8. STATISTICAL CONSIDERATIONS

8.1 Sample Size Determination

The sample size of 220 subjects (110 per treatment arm) provides approximately 90% power to detect a between-group difference of 5 percentage points in the change from baseline to Week 24 in LVEF, assuming a standard deviation of 11 percentage points and a two-sided significance level of 0.05. The calculation accounts for a 15% dropout rate.

8.2 Analysis Populations

The following analysis populations will be defined:

- Intent-to-Treat (ITT) Population: all randomised subjects. Subjects will be analysed according to the treatment arm to which they were randomised, regardless of the treatment actually received.
- Per-Protocol (PP) Population: all randomised subjects who complete the Week 24 visit, have no major protocol deviations that could affect the primary endpoint, and have a valid Week 24 LVEF measurement.
- Safety Population: all randomised subjects who receive at least one dose of study medication. Subjects will be analysed according to the treatment actually received.

8.3 Primary Efficacy Analysis

The primary efficacy endpoint is the change from baseline to Week 24 in LVEF, measured by echocardiography. The primary analysis will compare the change from baseline between the two treatment arms using an analysis of covariance (ANCOVA) model with treatment arm as a fixed effect and baseline LVEF as a covariate. The primary analysis will be performed on the ITT Population using a mixed-effects model for repeated measures (MMRM) to handle missing data; this approach replaces the earlier plan to use last observation carried forward (LOCF), which was superseded in Amendment 2. The MMRM will include the categorical effects of treatment, visit, and treatment-by-visit interaction, as well as the continuous covariates of baseline LVEF and baseline-by-visit interaction.

8.4 Secondary Analyses

Secondary endpoints will be analysed using similar MMRM or ANCOVA models, as appropriate for the endpoint type. Categorical endpoints will be analysed using a Cochran–Mantel–Haenszel test or logistic regression with adjustment for baseline value where applicable. Time-to-event endpoints will be analysed using a Cox proportional hazards model with treatment arm as a covariate.

**9. SAFETY MONITORING AND ADVERSE EVENT REPORTING**

**9.1 Definitions**

An **Adverse Event (AE)** is any untoward medical occurrence in a subject administered a study medication, which does not necessarily have a causal relationship with the treatment. An AE can therefore be any unfavourable and unintended sign (including an abnormal laboratory finding), symptom, or disease temporally associated with the use of a study medication, whether or not considered related to the study medication.

A **Serious Adverse Event (SAE)** is any AE that:
- Results in death,
- Is life-threatening (i.e., the subject was at immediate risk of death at the time of the event),
- Requires inpatient hospitalisation or prolongation of existing hospitalisation,
- Results in persistent or significant disability/incapacity,
- Is a congenital anomaly/birth defect, or
- Is a medically important event that may not be immediately life-threatening or result in death or hospitalisation but may jeopardise the subject or may require medical or surgical intervention to prevent one of the other outcomes listed above.

**9.2 Collection and Recording of Adverse Events**

All AEs occurring from the time of informed consent until 30 days after the last dose of study medication will be collected, recorded, and reported. After this period, only SAEs considered related to study medication should be reported to the Sponsor.

At each study visit, subjects will be asked a non-leading question about their well-being (e.g., "How have you been feeling since your last visit?"). All AEs, whether reported spontaneously by the subject or elicited by the investigator, will be recorded on the Adverse Event Case Report Form (CRF) page. The following information will be documented for each AE:

- Description of the event
- Date of onset and resolution
- Severity (Mild, Moderate, Severe)
- Relationship to study medication (Not Related, Unlikely, Possibly, Probably, Definitely)
- Action taken with study medication (None, Dose Reduced, Drug Interrupted, Drug Withdrawn)
- Outcome (Recovered, Recovering, Not Recovered, Recovered with Sequelae, Fatal)
- Whether the event is serious

AEs will be graded for severity using the CTCAE v5.0 criteria. For events not listed in CTCAE v5.0, the following definitions apply:
- **Mild:** Transient or mild discomfort; no limitation in normal daily activities; no medical intervention required.
- **Moderate:** Some limitation in normal daily activities; minimal medical intervention required.
- **Severe:** Marked limitation in normal daily activities; medical intervention and/or hospitalisation required.

The relationship of an AE to study medication will be assessed by the investigator, taking into account the temporal relationship, dechallenge/rechallenge information, and the presence of a more likely alternative explanation (e.g., underlying disease, concomitant medication).

**9.3 Serious Adverse Event Reporting**

All SAEs must be reported to the Sponsor (or its designee) within **24 hours** of the site becoming aware of the event. The initial report may be made by telephone or email, and must be followed by a written SAE report on the SAE form provided by the Sponsor. The SAE form should be completed and submitted within **3 calendar days** of the initial report.

1. BACKGROUND AND RATIONALE

Asthma is a chronic inflammatory airway disease affecting an estimated 5–8% of adults in Singapore. Despite the availability of effective inhaled therapies, a substantial proportion of patients remain uncontrolled, experiencing frequent symptoms, exacerbations, and impaired quality of life. Uncontrolled asthma is associated with significant healthcare utilisation, including emergency department visits and hospitalisations, particularly in severe disease.

RESP-107 is a novel inhaled small-molecule modulator of the prostaglandin D2 receptor (DP2/CRTH2) developed by SCRI. Unlike systemic DP2 antagonists that have shown mixed results in prior trials, RESP-107 is designed for targeted airway delivery via a dry powder inhaler (DPI), potentially achieving high local concentrations with reduced systemic exposure. Preclinical studies in murine and primate models demonstrated dose-dependent reduction in airway eosinophilia, mucus hypersecretion, and airway hyperresponsiveness following allergen challenge. Phase 1 studies in healthy volunteers and mild asthmatics showed acceptable tolerability and a pharmacokinetic profile supportive of twice-daily dosing.

The rationale for evaluating RESP-107 in uncontrolled moderate-to-severe asthma is based on the recognised role of prostaglandin D2 in type-2 airway inflammation. Recruitment of eosinophils, mast cells, and Th2 lymphocytes via DP2 contributes to persistent airway inflammation despite ICS/LABA therapy. By antagonising DP2 at the airway level, RESP-107 may offer a novel non-steroidal add-on mechanism to improve asthma control and reduce exacerbation risk.

This study aims to evaluate the efficacy, safety, and pharmacokinetics of two doses of inhaled RESP-107 compared with placebo when added to standard-of-care ICS/LABA background therapy in adults with uncontrolled moderate-to-severe asthma. The results will inform dose selection for subsequent Phase 3 development.

Participants meeting any of the following criteria at Screening or Randomisation are not eligible for study participation:

1. Life-threatening asthma within 12 months prior to Screening, defined as an asthma episode requiring intubation, mechanical ventilation, or associated with hypercapnia or respiratory arrest.
2. Asthma exacerbation requiring systemic corticosteroids within 4 weeks prior to Screening (Visit 1).
3. Respiratory tract infection (upper or lower) within 4 weeks prior to Screening.
4. Clinically significant non-asthma pulmonary disease, including but not limited to chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), bronchiectasis, interstitial lung disease, or alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency.
5. Current smoker, or smoking history of more than 10 pack-years.
6. Known hypersensitivity or contraindication to RESP-107 or any of its excipients, or to any of the rescue or background medications used in the study.
7. Use of systemic corticosteroids (oral, parenteral, or high-dose inhaled) within 4 weeks prior to Screening.
8. Use of biologic therapies (e.g., anti-IgE, anti-IL5, anti-IL4Rα, anti-TSLP) within 6 months or 5 half-lives (whichever is longer) prior to Screening.
9. Use of any investigational drug or device within 30 days or 5 half-lives (whichever is longer) prior to Screening.
10. History of malignancy within 5 years prior to Screening, except for adequately treated non-melanoma skin cancer or carcinoma in situ of the cervix.
11. Clinically significant cardiovascular, hepatic, renal, neurological, psychiatric, or haematological disease that, in the opinion of the Investigator, could interfere with the participant’s safety, compliance, or the interpretation of study results.
12. Alanine aminotransferase (ALT) or aspartate aminotransferase (AST) > 2.5 × upper limit of normal (ULN), or total bilirubin > 1.5 × ULN at Screening.
13. Estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) < 45 mL/min/1.73 m² at Screening, calculated using the CKD-EPI equation.
14. Pregnant or lactating women, or women of childbearing potential who are not willing to use a highly effective method of contraception during the study and for 30 days after the last dose of study drug.
15. Known or suspected alcohol or drug abuse within 12 months prior to Screening.
16. Any other condition that, in the opinion of the Investigator or the Sponsor, would make the participant unsuitable for the study.

6.3 Screening and Run-in Period

Potential participants will undergo screening assessments within 28 days prior to the start of the run-in period. The run-in period is 2 weeks (± 3 days). During the run-in period, participants will continue their usual ICS/LABA background therapy and will be instructed on the use of the eDiary to record daily asthma symptoms, rescue medication use, and morning peak expiratory flow (PEF). Participants will also receive a short-acting beta-agonist (SABA) for rescue use.

Compliance with eDiary completion and study procedures during the run-in period will be assessed prior to randomisation. 7.1 Overall Design

This is a Phase 2b, randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled, parallel-group, multicentre study to evaluate the efficacy, safety, and pharmacokinetics of two doses of inhaled RESP-107 compared with placebo in adults with uncontrolled moderate-to-severe asthma on background ICS/LABA therapy.

9. STATISTICAL METHODS

9.1 Sample Size Determination

The sample size was calculated based on the primary endpoint of change from Baseline in pre-dose trough FEV1 at Week 12. A total of 240 participants will be randomised in a 1:1:1 ratio to receive RESP-107 100 mg once daily, RESP-107 200 mg once daily, or placebo. This provides 80 participants per treatment group.

The assumed treatment difference versus placebo is 120 mL in the change from Baseline in pre-dose trough FEV1 at Week 12, with a common standard deviation of 250 mL. Using a two-sided t-test at the 5% significance level, 80 participants per group provides approximately 90% power to detect this difference. No adjustment for multiplicity is required for the primary endpoint because there is only one primary comparison of interest (each active dose versus placebo). The secondary endpoints will be analysed hierarchically to control the family-wise error rate.

The sample size of 240 participants also allows for a discontinuation rate of approximately 15% over the 12-week treatment period. If more participants than expected discontinue, the sponsor may consider enrolling additional participants up to a maximum of 270, provided that the additional enrolment does not compromise the study timeline. Any decision to enrol beyond 240 participants must be documented in a protocol deviation log and approved by the Medical Monitor.

9.1.1 Re-estimation of Sample Size

No formal sample size re-estimation is planned. The sample size is fixed at the time of protocol approval. If the observed standard deviation at the interim analysis (if any) suggests that the study is underpowered, the sponsor will discuss with the Data Safety Monitoring Board (DSMB) whether to continue the study as planned or to make a recommendation to the ethics committee.

9.2 Analysis Populations

The following analysis populations are defined:

1. Intent-to-Treat (ITT) Population: All randomised participants who receive at least one dose of study drug. Participants will be analysed according to the treatment group to which they were randomised, regardless of the treatment actually received. This population will be used for the primary efficacy analysis.

2. Per-Protocol (PP) Population: A subset of the ITT population who complete the study without any major protocol deviations. Major protocol deviations include, but are not limited to: receipt of the wrong treatment, use of prohibited concomitant medication, or missing the Week 12 visit. This population will be used for sensitivity analyses.

3. Safety Population: All randomised participants who receive at least one dose of study drug. Participants will be analysed according to the treatment actually received. This population will be used for all safety analyses.

4. PK Population: All participants in the PK substudy who receive at least one dose of study drug and have at least one evaluable PK sample. This population will be used for all pharmacokinetic analyses.

Participants who are randomised but do not receive any dose of study drug will be excluded from all analysis populations. A listing of all randomised participants will be provided, with the reason for exclusion from each population documented.

10. SAFETY MONITORING AND REPORTING

10.1 General

The Investigator is responsible for ensuring the safety of all participants enrolled at the site. All adverse events (AEs), whether observed by the Investigator or reported by the participant, will be recorded in the participant's source documents and on the electronic Case Report Form (eCRF). The recording period for AEs begins after the participant has signed the informed consent form and ends 30 days after the last dose of study drug, or at the Week 12 visit, whichever occurs later.

Any AE that is ongoing at the end of the recording period will be followed until resolution, stabilisation, or until the Investigator determines that further follow-up is not clinically warranted. The reason for discontinuation of follow-up will be documented.

10.2 Definitions

10.2.1 Adverse Event (AE)

An AE is any untoward medical occurrence in a participant administered a study drug, which does not necessarily have a causal relationship with the treatment. An AE can therefore be any unfavourable and unintended sign (including an abnormal laboratory finding), symptom, or disease temporally associated with the use of a study drug, whether or not considered related to the study drug.

10.2.2 Serious Adverse Event (SAE)

An SAE is any untoward medical occurrence that, at any dose:

- Results in death;
- Is life-threatening (i.e., the participant was at immediate risk of death at the time of the event; this does not include an event that, had it occurred in a more severe form, might have caused death);
- Requires inpatient hospitalisation or prolongation of existing hospitalisation;
- Results in persistent or significant disability/incapacity;
- Is a congenital anomaly/birth defect; or
- Is a medically important event that, based on medical or scientific judgement, may jeopardise the participant or may require medical or surgical intervention to prevent one of the outcomes listed above.

10.2.3 Adverse Event of Special Interest (AESI)

The following events are considered AESIs for this study:

- Symptomatic bradycardia (heart rate < 45 bpm with associated symptoms);
- Second- or third-degree atrioventricular block;
- New-onset atrial fibrillation or flutter;
- Acute respiratory distress syndrome;
- Anaphylaxis or severe hypersensitivity reaction.

AESIs do not necessarily meet the criteria for seriousness but will be reported to the sponsor within 24 hours of the site becoming aware of the event.

10.3 Assessment of Causality and Severity

The Investigator will assess the relationship of each AE to the study drug using the following categories: Not Related, Unlikely Related, Possibly Related, Probably Related, or Definitely Related. The relationship assessment will be based on the temporal relationship, pharmacological plausibility, and the existence of an alternative aetiology.

The severity of each AE will be graded according to the Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events (CTCAE) version 5.0, as follows:

| Grade | Term            | Description                                                      |
|-------|-----------------|------------------------------------------------------------------|
| 1     | Mild            | Asymptomatic or mild symptoms; clinical or diagnostic observations only; intervention not indicated. |
| 2     | Moderate        | Minimal, local, or non-invasive intervention indicated; limiting age-appropriate instrumental activities of daily living. |
| 3     | Severe          | Medically significant but not immediately life-threatening; hospitalisation or prolongation of hospitalisation indicated; disabling. |
| 4     | Life-threatening| Urgent intervention indicated.                                   |
| 5     | Death related to AE | Fatal.                                                       |
